questions.prompt: What do we call a named place in a program that stores a value which can change while the program runs?
questions.explain: A variable stores a value that can be updated as the program runs, unlike a fixed number written directly into the code.

questions.prompt: A variable called count starts at 0. A loop adds 3 to it, five times in a row. What does count equal by the end?
questions.explain: Adding 3 five times is 3 x 5 = 15, so count ends at 0 + 15 = 15.

questions.prompt: A variable called total starts at 10. A loop subtracts 2 from it, four times in a row. What does total equal by the end?
questions.explain: Subtracting 2 four times is 2 x 4 = 8, so total ends at 10 - 8 = 2.

questions.prompt: Which everyday action below is actually an example of a loop - repeating the same step for each of several things?
choices: Placing one fork at each of the 6 seats at the table, one after another
Turning the oven on once
Answering the phone one time
Locking the front door
questions.answer: Placing one fork at each of the 6 seats at the table, one after another
questions.explain: Repeating the same action once for each of several items is exactly what a loop does.

questions.prompt: Instead of writing the same instruction out 10 separate times, a programmer puts it inside a loop once. Why?
choices: It's shorter, easier to read, and only needs fixing in one place if something changes
It makes the program run on more devices
It automatically fixes all bugs
It uses more electricity, which is more efficient
questions.answer: It's shorter, easier to read, and only needs fixing in one place if something changes
questions.explain: A loop keeps the repeated instruction in one place, so changing or fixing it only has to happen once.

questions.prompt: A loop is supposed to water 10 plants, one cup each, but ends up watering only 9 because a variable started at the wrong number. What's this specific, well-known kind of bug called?
questions.explain: Running one repeat too few (or too many) because the start or stop point is set incorrectly is the classic off-by-one error.

questions.prompt: Someone claims a variable, once set, can never change for the rest of the program's life. Are they right?
questions.explain: The whole point of a variable is that its value can change while the program runs - that's what makes it different from a fixed value.

questions.prompt: A variable score starts at 0 and a variable lives starts at 3. A loop runs up to 4 times. Each time through: lives decreases by 1 and score increases by 5, UNLESS lives would go below 0, in which case lives stays at 0 and the loop stops immediately without adding more score that round. What is the final value of score once the loop finishes or stops?
questions.explain: Round 1: lives 3-1=2, score 0+5=5. Round 2: lives 2-1=1, score 5+5=10. Round 3: lives 1-1=0, score 10+5=15. Round 4: lives would go to -1, which isn't allowed, so lives stays 0 and no more score is added. Final score is 15.

questions.prompt: A loop runs once per day for 5 days. Each day, total_sales = total_sales + (items sold that day x $2), starting from total_sales = 0. Items sold each day: 3, 5, 2, 4, 6. What is total_sales after all 5 days?
questions.explain: Total items sold: 3+5+2+4+6 = 20. Multiplying by $2 per item: 20 x 2 = $40.

questions.prompt: A robot is meant to water 15 plants, one cup each, by looping from plant 1 to plant 15. Because of an off-by-one bug, the loop actually starts counting from plant 2 and still stops at plant 15. How many plants actually get watered?
questions.explain: Counting from plant 2 through to plant 15 inclusive is 14 plants (15-2+1=14), one fewer than the intended 15, because of the shifted starting point.

questions.prompt: An outer loop runs 3 times. Each time, it runs an inner loop that adds 1 to a variable called count, 4 times. If count starts at 0, what is count after the outer loop finishes all 3 rounds?
questions.explain: Each outer round runs the inner loop 4 times, adding 4 to count. Over 3 outer rounds: 4 x 3 = 12.

activity.title: Run your own physical loop experiment: repeat, time and average
activity.why: Proves they can act as 'the computer' running a loop with a real counting variable, and use the looped results to calculate something real, not just recite the definition of a loop.
steps: Choose a simple repeated action (e.g. star jumps, hopping on one foot, stacking 5 cups and knocking them down).
Start a loop counter at 0, either in your head or on paper.
Repeat the action exactly 8 times, timing each single repeat with a stopwatch, and write down each of the 8 times in seconds.
After each repeat, add 1 to your counter and say the count out loud, exactly like a loop would.
Once you have all 8 times, add them up and divide by 8 to find the mean time per repeat.
Record your total time, your mean, and your fastest repeat below.

record.label: What was the total time, in seconds, for all 8 repeats added together?
What was the mean time per repeat, to 1 decimal place, in seconds?
What was your fastest single repeat, in seconds?
Did your times get faster or slower as you repeated the loop more times? What do you think caused that?
What action did you repeat?

activity.check: The mean time should equal the total time divided by 8, and the fastest time should be less than or equal to the mean. Query it if the mean is smaller than the fastest single repeat, which isn't mathematically possible.

lessons.title: Scams, phishing and clickbait: the pressure signals that give them away
lessons.intro: Scammers don't need to trick a computer - they need to trick a person, fast, before you stop and think. Once you know the pressure signals, they get a lot easier to spot.

sections.heading: What is phishing?
sections.body: **Phishing** is a fake message - an email, text or chat - pretending to be from someone trustworthy, trying to trick you into giving up personal information, passwords, or money, or into clicking a dangerous link.

sections.heading: The pressure signals
sections.body:
Scam messages tend to use the same handful of tricks to stop you thinking too carefully:

- **Urgency** - "act in the next 10 minutes or lose your account"
- **Too good to be true** - "you've won a prize you never entered"
- **Requests for secrecy or personal info** - asking you to keep it quiet, or to hand over a password
- **A sender name that's slightly wrong** - close to a real one, but not quite
- **Spelling and grammar mistakes** that a real organisation usually wouldn't make

sections.heading: Checking a link before you trust it
sections.body: The words a link shows and the real web address underneath don't always match. If a link's visible text says a familiar website, but the actual address looks different or slightly misspelled, that's a red flag. The safest move is not to click - instead, type the real address in yourself, or ask a trusted adult to check it with you.

sections.heading: What real organisations don't do
sections.body: As a general rule, a genuine organisation won't ask you to send your password by message or email, and won't pressure you to act within the next few minutes. If a message is doing either of those things, treat it with suspicion.

key_points: Phishing is a fake message trying to trick you into giving up information, money, or clicking a dangerous link.
Common pressure signals include urgency, too-good-to-be-true offers, and requests for secrecy.
A link's visible text and its real underlying address don't always match - check before clicking.
A genuine organisation won't ask you to send your password by message or email.
Several pressure signals appearing together is a strong sign a message is a scam.
lessons.try_this: With a trusted adult, look together at an old email or message in the family inbox (a real one, or make up an example) and go through the pressure-signal checklist: is it urgent? too good to be true? asking for personal info? Does the sender look right?

questions.prompt: A message that says 'act now or lose your account in the next 10 minutes' is using urgency to pressure you.
questions.explain: Creating a false sense of urgency is a classic scam tactic, meant to stop you from stopping to check whether the message is real.

questions.prompt: What is 'phishing'?
choices: A fake message trying to trick you into giving up personal information or clicking a dangerous link
A type of computer virus that damages hardware
A legitimate way websites ask for your password
A way to catch real fish using an app
questions.answer: A fake message trying to trick you into giving up personal information or clicking a dangerous link
questions.explain: Phishing messages pretend to be from someone trustworthy to trick you into handing over information or clicking something dangerous.

questions.prompt: A message lands in your inbox. Which detail below would actually be a warning sign that it's a scam?
choices: It pressures you to act immediately or something bad will happen
It's from someone whose name you clearly recognise, with no rush and no requests
It arrived during normal daytime hours
It's written in plain, simple language
questions.answer: It pressures you to act immediately or something bad will happen
questions.explain: Urgency is one of the main pressure signals scammers use to stop you from thinking it through.

questions.prompt: A message says you've won a prize you never entered, and asks you to click a link and type in your password to claim it. What's the best response?
choices: Don't click the link, and check with a trusted adult before doing anything
Click the link straight away to see what you've won
Reply asking for more details about the prize
Forward it to friends so they can check if it's real
questions.answer: Don't click the link, and check with a trusted adult before doing anything
questions.explain: A prize you never entered, combined with a request for your password, is a classic phishing pattern - the safest move is not to click and to check with a trusted adult.

questions.prompt: A message claims to be from your bank and asks you to reply with your password to 'verify your account'. Would a genuine, real bank ever actually ask for your password this way?
questions.explain: Genuine organisations don't need your actual password sent to them - a request like this is a strong warning sign.

questions.prompt: A headline screams 'YOU WON'T BELIEVE WHAT HAPPENED NEXT!' but the article barely mentions it. What's this kind of headline called?
questions.explain: Clickbait headlines are designed to be tempting to click, even when the actual content doesn't live up to the promise.

questions.prompt: A message is urgent, asks for your personal details, and comes from a sender you don't recognise. What does this combination of signals suggest?
questions.explain: The more pressure signals a message stacks together, the more likely it is to be a scam.

questions.prompt: A link's visible text reads a familiar website's name, but the actual address underneath it looks different and slightly misspelled. Is that a reason to be suspicious?
questions.explain: A mismatch between what a link says and where it actually leads is a common trick used in phishing messages.

questions.prompt: A message reads: 'URGENT!! Act within 15 minutes or your account will be LOCKED forever. Congratulations - you have been chosen to recieve a $500 prize you never entered for! Just reply with your password to claim it now.' Counting from this list - urgency, too-good-to-be-true, a request for personal info, and a spelling mistake - how many separate types of pressure signal appear in this one message?
questions.explain: This single message stacks urgency ('within 15 minutes'), a too-good-to-be-true prize, a direct request for a password, and a spelling mistake ('recieve') - all four signals at once, which is a very strong sign of a scam.

questions.prompt: A link's visible text says 'www.commbank.com.au' but the real address underneath is 'www.comm-bank-secure-login.ru'. How many separate suspicious differences can you count between the visible text and the real address (extra inserted words, and a different domain ending)?
questions.explain: There are two separate red flags: extra words have been inserted ('-secure-login'), and the domain ending is different ('.ru' instead of '.com.au'). Either one alone is worth checking; together they're a strong warning.

questions.prompt: In a scam message offering a $500 prize you never entered, which single pressure signal would be most alarming from a genuine organisation, because it directly asks for something a real organisation never requests?
questions.explain: A genuine organisation will never ask you to send your actual password by message or email - that request alone is enough to treat the whole message as a scam.

questions.prompt: A message claims to be from 'Telstra Suport Team' (note the misspelling), asks you to click a link to 'verify your account in the next 5 minutes', and shows link text of 'telstra.com.au' that actually leads to a jumble of random letters. How many of these 3 warning signs (misspelled sender name, urgency, mismatched link address) does this one message contain?
questions.explain: All three signs are present at once: the misspelled sender name ('Suport'), the urgency ('next 5 minutes'), and the link text not matching the real destination. Multiple signals stacking together is a very strong indicator of a scam.

activity.title: Score three real messages from the family inbox against the pressure-signal checklist
activity.why: Proves they can spot and count real pressure signals in messages nobody wrote specially for this lesson, with a trusted adult checking their work.
materials: a parent's email or message inbox, looked at together
steps: With a parent, open the family email or messages together and find 3 real messages - everyday ones (a receipt, a newsletter) or a genuine bit of spam if there is one. Never click any links or reply to anything.

For each message, check off which of these 5 signals appear: urgency, too-good-to-be-true, a request for personal info or a password, a sender name that looks slightly wrong, and spelling or grammar mistakes.
Count how many of the 5 signals each message has, and write a score from 0 to 5 next to each one.
Add up the total score across all 3 messages.
Pick the highest-scoring message and, with your parent, decide together what the safest response to it would have been.
Record your results below.

record.label: How many messages did you check?
What was the combined signal score across all 3 messages, out of 15?
What was the score of your highest-scoring single message, out of 5?
For your highest-scoring message, what did you and your parent decide the safest response would have been?
Who did you check the inbox with?

activity.check: The total_signal_score should equal the sum of individual scores across the 3 messages checked, and no link should have actually been clicked or replied to during this activity. Query it if it wasn't done with a parent present.

lessons.title: AI and the internet: what a chatbot actually does, why it can be confidently wrong, and how to check it
lessons.intro: Chatbots can sound calm, confident and sure of themselves - even when they're completely wrong. Understanding roughly how they work is what lets you use them without being fooled by them.

sections.heading: What a chatbot is actually doing
sections.body: A chatbot has been trained on huge amounts of text, and it works by predicting the most likely next words to write, based on patterns it learned. It isn't looking facts up in real time the way a search engine does, and it doesn't "know" things the way a person does - it's generating text that fits the patterns it learned.

sections.heading: Confident and wrong at the same time
sections.body: A **hallucination** is when an AI states something false as if it were completely true, with no obvious sign that it's unsure. This can include made-up facts, dates, quotes, or even sources that sound completely real but don't actually exist.

sections.heading: Checking before you trust it
sections.body: Treat a chatbot's answer as a starting point, not a final answer - especially for facts, dates, numbers, or anything going into schoolwork. Check important claims against another reliable source before using them.

example.prompt: A chatbot tells you a historical event happened in a specific year, and you want to use that date in a school project. What should you do first?
working: Don't assume the confident tone means it's correct
Look up the date in another reliable source, like a textbook or trusted website
example.answer: Check the date against another reliable source before using it

sections.heading: What chatbots are and aren't good for
sections.body: Chatbots can be genuinely useful for brainstorming ideas, explaining a concept in a different way, or drafting something you'll edit yourself. They're riskier for anything where getting an exact fact wrong actually matters - dates, statistics, quotes - unless you check it against another source.

key_points: A chatbot predicts likely next words based on patterns it learned, rather than looking facts up or 'knowing' them.
A hallucination is when an AI confidently states something false as if it were true.
A confident tone is not proof that an answer is correct.
Always check important facts, dates or numbers against another reliable source.
Chatbots are useful for brainstorming and drafting, but riskier for exact facts unless you verify them.
lessons.try_this: Ask a chatbot a question you already know the answer to (like a fact from a school topic or a family fact), and compare its answer word-for-word with what you know is true. Talk with a family member about anything it got wrong or made sound more certain than it should have.

questions.prompt: A chatbot can sometimes sound very confident while being completely wrong.
questions.explain: A chatbot's tone doesn't change based on whether it's actually correct - it can state a wrong answer just as confidently as a right one.

questions.prompt: What should you do with an important fact a chatbot gives you before using it in schoolwork?
choices: Check it against another reliable source
Trust it completely because it sounded confident
Assume it's wrong just because it came from a chatbot
Only use it if it's written in bold
questions.answer: Check it against another reliable source
questions.explain: Checking important facts against another reliable source is the safest way to catch a chatbot mistake before it ends up in your work.

questions.prompt: A chatbot writes a reply almost instantly, without ever pausing to search the internet. Roughly how does it actually decide what to write?
choices: It predicts likely next words based on patterns it learned from huge amounts of text
It looks every fact up on the internet in real time, like a search engine, before every reply
It phones a real person who checks each answer
It randomly guesses letters until they form real words
questions.answer: It predicts likely next words based on patterns it learned from huge amounts of text
questions.explain: A chatbot generates text by predicting likely next words from patterns in what it was trained on, not by looking things up live.

questions.prompt: A chatbot states a made-up date as fact, sounding just as sure as when it's right. What's this specific behaviour called?
questions.explain: A hallucination is a confidently stated but false claim from an AI, with no obvious sign that it's unsure.

questions.prompt: A chatbot answers a question in a calm, confident tone. Does that tone actually prove the answer is correct?
questions.explain: Tone and accuracy aren't connected - a chatbot can sound just as confident when it's wrong as when it's right.

questions.prompt: You're deciding whether to trust a chatbot's help without double-checking it. For which of these is that actually safer?
choices: Brainstorming ideas for a story you'll write yourself
Giving you the exact date of a historical event for a school project
Telling you an exact statistic to quote as fact
Confirming a fact you plan to repeat without checking
questions.answer: Brainstorming ideas for a story you'll write yourself
questions.explain: Brainstorming is low-stakes and creative, unlike exact facts, dates or statistics, which need checking before you rely on them.

questions.prompt: A chatbot gives you a specific historical date for a school project. What's the best approach before using it?
answer: check it against another reliable source
questions.explain: Checking against an independent, reliable source is the only reliable way to confirm a fact a chatbot gives you.

questions.prompt: Because a chatbot is a computer program, someone argues everything it says must automatically be true. Are they right?
questions.explain: Being a computer program doesn't make an output true - chatbots can and do generate confidently wrong information.

questions.prompt: A chatbot claims: 'Population grew from 2,000 to 2,800, an increase of 50%.' Check the chatbot's own numbers: what is the ACTUAL percentage increase from 2,000 to 2,800?
questions.explain: The real increase is (2800-2000) divided by 2000 = 800/2000 = 0.4, which is 40%, not the 50% the chatbot confidently stated. Checking a claim's own arithmetic is one of the fastest ways to catch a hallucination.

questions.prompt: A chatbot gives you 3 'facts' for a school project. You check them: fact 1 is correct, fact 2 is wrong, fact 3 is correct. What percentage of the 3 facts turned out to be accurate?
questions.explain: 2 out of 3 facts checked out correctly. 2 divided by 3 = 0.6667, which is about 66.7%, meaning roughly a third of what sounded equally confident was actually wrong.

questions.prompt: A chatbot says: 'This frog lays 100 eggs per clutch, and a female lays 4 clutches a year, giving her about 300 eggs annually.' Check the chatbot's own arithmetic: what should the annual total actually be (100 eggs x 4 clutches)?
questions.explain: 100 x 4 = 400, not the 300 the chatbot stated. The individual numbers it gave (100 and 4) don't even match its own final claim, which is a clear internal inconsistency worth catching before repeating it.

questions.prompt: For a school project, a chatbot gave 6 total claims. 2 were brainstorming ideas (opinions, not facts), and the rest were treated as facts needing verification. Of those facts, only 3 were actually checked before the project was submitted. How many unverified 'facts' ended up in the final project?
questions.explain: 6 total claims minus 2 brainstorming ideas leaves 4 facts needing a check. Only 3 of those 4 were actually verified, so 1 unverified fact made it into the final project.

activity.title: Fact-check five chatbot claims against real books or trusted print sources
activity.why: Proves they can verify AI claims against independent sources and calculate real accuracy, rather than just trusting a confident-sounding answer.
materials: a chatbot, accessed briefly with a parent, just to generate 5 claims
a physical book, encyclopedia, atlas or other printed trusted source
steps: With a parent, ask a chatbot for 5 specific factual claims about a topic you're both curious about (e.g. animal facts, historical dates, geography) and write all 5 down on paper.
Put the screen away, then check each of the 5 claims against a real book, atlas, encyclopedia or other printed trusted source at home.
Mark each claim as correct or incorrect based on what your printed source says.
Count how many of the 5 claims were correct, and work out that as a percentage.
For any claim that was wrong, write down what the printed source actually said instead.
Record your results below.

record.label: How many chatbot claims did you check?
How many of them were confirmed correct by your printed source?
What percentage of the claims were correct, to the nearest whole number?
Describe one claim that turned out wrong (or say 'none were wrong' if all were correct), and what the real answer was.
What printed source did you check against?

activity.check: correct_count should be no higher than claims_checked, and accuracy_percent should roughly equal correct_count divided by claims_checked as a percentage. Query it if the percentage doesn't match those two numbers.
